title: Listening in Mali Gaura
hookLine: listen to one hymn and its Bhagat verse

cards: Blessed is the wool. That's a line from the Guru Granth Sahib. Not blessed is the temple, not blessed is the king.

Blessed is the wool, and the blanket made from it. It comes near the end of Mali Gaura, in the first hymn of its guest, Bhagat Namdev. So today, reading along with him slowly: why would a saint bless a sheep's coat?

teach.b: Namdev's hymn starts with music. In plain English, not word for word: blessed, blessed is that flute the Lord plays; the sweet, sweet sound rings out, unstruck.
That line is marked Rahao, pause, and in Sikh reading the Rahao line is the center the rest of the hymn turns around. Then Namdev starts blessing things.
Blessed is the wool of the sheep. Blessed is the blanket Krishna wraps around himself. Blessed is mother Devaki, in whose home the Lord was born.
Blessed is the forest of Brindaban.

teach.h: FROM THE FLUTE OUT TO THE BLANKET.
teach.b: Namdev is singing from inside the stories of his own world, the cowherd Krishna with his flute, and Sikhs read these names as names for the one God the whole Granth praises. Watch the direction.

Namdev doesn't stay with the grand things. He goes to the wool, the blanket, a mother's house, a forest. The holy, in this hymn, makes everything near it holy too: the ordinary cloth, the ordinary home.

It's short enough to hear end to end in one sitting, and with the words in front of you, you can watch it walk outward from the flute to the wool. The word for sweet here is madhur, and Namdev doubles it: madhur madhur.
Mali Gaura was short and sweet. Namdev's verse is sweet and short.

how: Hymns of the Bhagats, like Namdev's, are sung in kirtan in their raga just as the Gurus' hymns are, and many listeners follow the Gurmukhi text with a translation on a screen or in a book while it is sung.

games.q: what does “listening in mali gaura” mean?
o: reading along slowly as Namdev's short hymn is sung
a silent sitting where no hymns are heard
singing Namdev's hymn without any music at all

games.q: what's inside the hymn — tap the pairs.
p: the guest voice in Mali Gaura

s: Namdev's hymn only blesses grand, holy places
he blesses the wool, the blanket, a mother's home and a forest.
in Sikh reading, the Rahao line is treated as the hymn's center
here it's the flute line: blessed is that flute, sweet, sweet.
Namdev's hymn is too long to hear in one sitting
it's short: you can hear it end to end in one sitting, and read along as the blessings stack up.

games.q: you're Namdev, singing of the Lord's flute. what do you bless next?
o: the wool, and the blanket made from it.
games.why: Namdev turns to the ordinary: blessed is the sheep's wool, blessed the blanket Krishna wears, blessed the mother's home.

practice: Let your eyes rest on whatever is closest, a sleeve, a cup, the chair, and notice it with care: where it came from, whose hands touched it before yours.
Namdev blessed wool and a blanket; let this ordinary thing be quietly important for a minute. If you pray, say Waheguru as you look at it; if you don't, just keep your attention on it, gently.

wordCard.voice: Listening in Mali Gaura. Reading along with Bhagat Namdev's verse: the flute's sweet, sweet sound, and blessings on the wool and the blanket. Today's word.

orig.note: madhur, sweet: Namdev doubles it for the flute's sound in Mali Gaura.

carryVoice: Your line: sweet and short. In Namdev's hymn, even a blanket sits close to the holy. More tomorrow.
